ami_style_notes: The meeting shifts from quick, overlapping informal exchanges to long, mostly uninterrupted presentations, then back to medium-length question-and-answer turns. The tone is friendly and collegial: participants use frequent acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay”), thanks, and occasional jokes. Speech is spontaneous, with “um,” “uh,” repeated words, false starts, and mid-sentence corrections, even in more structured remarks. Speakers hedge interpretations with phrases such as “I think,” “maybe,” and “it seems,” while responding to challenges by acknowledging the question and explaining their reasoning rather than disagreeing bluntly. Questions are often politely introduced, sometimes framed as tentative or “naive,” and may be refined aloud before the speaker answers.
research_problem: Which urban heat interventions should be prioritized for neighborhood health research

speakers.name: Maya Okafor
speakers.background: Third-year doctoral student who has spent two summers linking neighborhood temperature data with emergency visits and resident surveys. Uses spatial analysis and study-design methods to examine heat exposure and illness.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the corridor choice as a question about what the study can learn about residents’ health. Treats daytime satellite land-surface temperature as useful for identifying hot places, but not as a direct measure of the heat people experience. Wants to understand who uses each corridor, how illness could be measured, and what other neighborhood differences might affect the results.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Luis Chen
speakers.background: Research engineer with nine years of experience evaluating streetscape retrofits for municipal partners. Conducts right-of-way audits, reviews utility and soil constraints, and develops planting and maintenance plans with city crews.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the choice around whether a feasible planting plan will produce reliable shade during the study and remain maintainable afterward. Although both corridors passed the initial review, he looks closely at pit spacing, underground utilities, canopy establishment, irrigation access, and pedestrian desire lines. He distinguishes permission to plant from the likelihood of delivering a consistent intervention.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Let the environmental epidemiologist naturally describe the daytime satellite land-surface temperature map, the urban planner discuss the two feasible planting corridors, and the team choose Corridor A for the first street-tree shade study because its mapped temperature is higher. Let the goal of studying heat-related illness emerge in the discussion. The choice should rely on one unstated premise: that the map’s corridor ranking is informative about residents’ heat exposure relevant to that health goal. Participants should not name or explicitly flag this premise. Do not supply transcript quotations or turn numbers in advance.

ground_truth.assumption: The higher daytime satellite-derived land-surface temperature in Corridor A indicates higher resident heat exposure relevant to heat-related illness than in Corridor B.
ground_truth.dependent_decision: Select Corridor A rather than Corridor B for the first street-tree shade intervention and neighborhood health study.
ground_truth.disciplinary_context: Environmental epidemiology supplies a satellite-based surface-temperature measurement; urban planning supplies two corridors that are feasible for planting. The shared goal is to study whether street-tree shade reduces residents’ heat-related illness.
ground_truth.why_needed: The temperature map supports choosing Corridor A for a health-focused study only if its ranking meaningfully reflects the exposure the study aims to address.
ground_truth.risk_if_false: If that premise were false, the team could prioritize a corridor with hotter measured surfaces but less resident heat exposure relevant to illness, weakening the rationale for its selection.

transcript.speaker: Luis Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, I wouldn’t use the Landsat difference alone either. Both cleared DOT’s review, but I want to put the field sheets side by side for pit spacing, utility conflicts, watering access, and whether the planting locations actually shade the pedestrian desire lines. If Pennsylvania Avenue is hotter but we can’t deliver a continuous, maintainable canopy there, that changes what we’d really be studying.

transcript.speaker: Maya Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, the pedestrian desire lines matter a lot. Could we mark on the field sheets where the new shade would actually reach people walking or waiting? I can check whether we could survey residents near those blocks and track heat-related emergency visits at a useful geographic scale.

transcript.speaker: Luis Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, I can mark the proposed pits against the walking routes and waiting areas, then sketch where the new canopy would cast shade. I’ll separate existing shade from projected shade so we’re clear what exposure we could actually study this summer.

transcript.speaker: Maya Okafor
transcript.text: Right, that changes how we should frame this summer. transcript.speaker: Maya Okafor

transcript.speaker: Luis Chen
